## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāvāṇijajātaka* (Ja 493) is a canonical narrative in the Jātaka collection whose verse opening is preserved as *Vāṇijā samitiṁ katvā* [Fausböll 1887]. The story was delivered by the Buddha while staying at Jetavana near Sāvatthī, prompted by an occasion concerning local merchants [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. The narrative recounts a caravan of merchants who lose their way in the wilderness and discover a magical, wish-fulfilling banyan tree [Buddhist Approach to Environmental Crisis 2009; Fausböll 1887]. Cutting its branches in different directions, they receive water, food, attendant maidens, and precious treasures [Buddhist Approach to Environmental Crisis 2009]. Blinded by insatiable greed (*lobha*), the merchants decide to uproot the tree entirely, ignoring the protests of one traveler who reminds them that one must not harm a benefactor that offered them shade and life [Buddhist Approach to Environmental Crisis 2009; Fausböll 1887]. Their ingratitude leads to their destruction, while the prudent caravan leader is spared [Buddhist Approach to Environmental Crisis 2009; Fausböll 1887]. In the conclusion of the story (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the Nāga king of the past as Sāriputta and himself as the wise caravan leader (*satthavāha*) [Fausböll 1887].

SuttaCentral records passage-level doctrinal and thematic parallels across several early Buddhist collections, including the *Taṇhuppādasutta* (AN 4.9), two discourses in the Itivuttaka (Iti 15, Iti 105), the *Dvayatānupassanā Sutta* (Snp 3.12), other Jātaka stories (Ja 452, Ja 528, Ja 538, Ja 546), and Chinese parallels in the Ekottarikāgama (SF 199, T 765.2), with additional echoes in several Therāpadāna poems (Tha-Ap 3, 8, 24, 474, 562) and a mention in the *Aṅkurapetavatthu* (Pv 21) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus documents comprehensive Pali-internal reuse across 25 segments matching the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Volume 4), edited by V. Fausböll [DharmaNexus; Fausböll 1887]. DharmaNexus also detects cross-language alignments with the Tibetan translation of the *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* (D4155) and the Chinese *Da zheng ju wang jing* (T 45) [DharmaNexus].
